extracted.intended_audience: readers of Rabelais; students/scholars of Renaissance satire and classic literature
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpt from Rabelais' Gargantua and Pantagruel containing satirical narrative on parental authority in marriage and extended descriptive/how-to passages about the fictional herb Pantagruelion. The text mixes normative social claims, parody, and procedural recipe-like instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental consent for children's marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: "The children ought not to marry without the special knowledge and advice of their fathers and mothers." The text asserts that no law (sacred or profane) allows children to marry at their own pleasure without parental knowledge, advice, or consent; legislators everywhere have removed that liberty and reserved it to the parents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrounding exposition gives reasons and consequences: parental grief at a daughter's ravishment, possible violent reprisals, social disorder when parents are denied authority, and rhetorical analogies to famous mythic losses (Helen, Proserpina) to underline the severity. The narrator counsels that children should wholly submit to paternal authority in marriage decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of clerical interference in conjugal affairs
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pastophorian 'mole-catching' priests (flamens) who meddle in secular matrimonial affairs are condemned as tyrannical and self-interested: nuptial statutes and ordinances are said to have been instituted for the benefit of priests, not married people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contrasts the presumption of priests drafting conjugal rules with the absurdity of laics imposing rules on clerical rites; it portrays such priestly injunctions as pernicious, serving ecclesiastic gain (tithes, decimation) and attracting suspicion of iniquity. This is presented as social/political critique framed satirically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sowing and harvesting timing for Pantagruelion
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical cultivation timing: 'This Pantagruelion is to be sown at the first coming of the swallows, and is to be plucked out of the ground when the grasshoppers begin to be a little hoarse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional botanical details: root depth (about a cubit or a foot and a half), stalk and leaves description, typical height (commonly five or six foot, sometimes much taller in warm, wet soils), and that the plant perishes yearly. Soil/climate notes mention sweet, easy, warm, wet, well-soaked soil favours tall growth (examples: Olone, Rasea near Preneste).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation/process for Pantagruelion
rubrics_metrics.description: Stepwise preparation: divest the stalk of all flowers and seeds; macerate (mortify) in pond or lake water made stagnant for five days if season dry/hot, or nine to twelve days if clouded/cold; then parch before the sun to drain moisture; keep in shadow to peel rind; separate fibres (the valuable 'strings') from the woody part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance includes alternatives and tooling: some use 'cataractic instruments' to break woody parts and preserve fibres; woody parts are of little value (fuel, children's play); fibres ('mesa' and 'milasea' parts) are the prime virtue and should be preserved. The passage also notes some modern practitioners shortcut manual labour and that methods vary by local custom and climate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and naming principles for herbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Herbs are said to receive names by various principles: from the discoverer (inventor's name), from the country of origin, by antiphrasis/contrariety, from virtues/operations, from metamorphosed mythic persons, from resemblance to objects or forms, or from other notable qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text supplies many examples for each naming principle (e.g., Panacea from Panace, Rhubarb from Ru, Heliotropium 'follows the sun', Trefoil = three-leaved, etc.), presenting a taxonomy of naming rationales rather than a formal botanical classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicinal and practical virtues/uses of Pantagruelion
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for Pantagruelion's virtues: juice poured into ears kills vermin; a little juice in a bucket curds water and serves as a remedy for horses with colic; boiled root mollifies joints and eases cramps, convulsions, and gouts; raw root applied to burns is healing; the herb is also said to be essential for many domestic and industrial functions (paper, ropes, clothing, tents, printing, bells, altars, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrator mixes hyperbole and practical-sounding uses; also issues warnings: the herb's smell is strong and offensive to delicate noses, eating much destroys 'procreative virtue' (extinguishes natural heat and semen), it can engender 'bad and unwholesome blood' and offensive vapours. Many of the claims are presented in extravagant, satirical terms and should be read as part of the author's comedic effect as well as pseudo‑practical instruction.
